title: The Target Is Not the Host: Reading a Target Triple, and the Same Struct in Four Sizes

questions.question: What does the target triple x86_64-w64-mingw32 name?
options: A target: architecture, vendor and system, with the system last since the second part is not an operating system
questions.explanation: Three shapes of triple are accepted.

questions.question: What is odd about long on 64 bit Windows?
options: It is 32 bits, where it is 64 on 64 bit Linux, so code that uses long for a 64 bit value breaks only there

questions.question: The same struct was 40 bytes on x86_64, 32 on 32 bit ARM and 28 on i686. Why is i686 smaller than ARM?
options: 32 bit x86 aligns an eight byte field to 4, and 32 bit ARM to 8
questions.explanation: Alignment is part of the ABI.

questions.question: { char, int64 } holds only fixed width types. Why is it not safe to send as it is?
options: It is 16 bytes on the 64 bit targets and 12 on 32 bit x86, because of the int64's alignment
questions.explanation: Write each field out in a defined order and width.

questions.question: What should the parser do with a triple it cannot read?
options: Be invalid with no word sizes: a reader that guesses builds for the wrong machine without a word
questions.explanation: Nine malformed triples were all invalid.

questions.question: How do you check a struct's size on the real target?
options: A static_assert on sizeof in the header, compiled by the cross compiler, since the model here was never run on that machine
questions.explanation: The numbers for ARM and i686 are the rules applied, not measured.
